explanations.explanation: Asaph says these are things “…that we have heard and known and our fathers have relayed to us.” So this wasn't a secret he dug up in the attic. It was handed down, mouth to ear, like a family recipe nobody ever wrote down. Somebody's dad said it, and somebody's kid remembered it.

Good guess, friend, an old scroll sounds very dramatic. But Asaph never mentions one. He says these things were heard and known, and that “…our fathers have relayed…” them to the people. No dusty treasure hunt, just fathers talking.

Nope, nobody shows up at the door with a mystery announcement here. Asaph says his people heard and knew these things, and that “…our fathers have relayed to us.” It came from their own fathers, not from some guy passing through.

I get why you'd pick it, because he did just say "…hidden from the beginning…" But Asaph says the opposite about the children: “We will not hide them from their children…” These stories are meant to be shared, not locked in a cabinet. Hidden from the beginning doesn't mean hidden from the kids.

Right, because Asaph says, “We will not hide them from their children…” Instead they will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD, His might and the wonders He has performed. These stories are for sharing, loudly. Nobody's keeping this one a secret.

explanations.answer: So they'd put their confidence in God
explanations.explanation: Asaph says it right there: “…that they should put their confidence in God, not forgetting His works, but keeping His commandments.” Every generation hears the stories so they remember what God has done. Remembering is how you lean on Him. That's the whole point of the relay.

explanations.answer: So the nations would fear them
explanations.explanation: Asaph never says anything about the nations here. The reason he gives is “…that they should put their confidence in God, not forgetting His works, but keeping His commandments.” The stories are about trusting God, not about impressing the neighbors.

explanations.answer: So they'd never need a king
explanations.explanation: Kings don't come up in these verses at all, friend. What Asaph says is “…that they should put their confidence in God, not forgetting His works, but keeping His commandments.” The goal is trust in God, and nothing here says anything about who sits on a throne.

That's his word for them: “…a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose heart was not loyal, whose spirit was not faithful to God.” Asaph doesn't sugarcoat it. He wants the next generation to hear it plainly so they can choose differently. Stubborn is a hard word, but it's the one he picked.

Close in spirit, maybe, but those aren't Asaph's words. He calls the fathers “…a stubborn and rebellious generation…” He also says their hearts weren't loyal and their spirits weren't faithful to God. Nobody here is bragging, they're digging in their heels.

Asaph doesn't use those words, friend. He calls them “…a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose heart was not loyal…” The problem he names isn't a lack of muscle. It's a heart that wasn't loyal and a spirit that wasn't faithful to God.
Yep, he follows it up fast. Right after the archers turn back, Asaph says they “…refused to live by His law.” Verse 10 also says they didn't keep God's covenant.

Asaph really does say it. Right after the archers of Ephraim turn back, he says they “…failed to keep God’s covenant and refused to live by His law.” It comes in the very next verse. He doesn't leave it hanging.

Asaph says, “They forgot what He had done, the wonders He had shown them.” Forgetting is the heart of this whole psalm. I know a little about being forgotten, friend, and I wouldn't wish it on a wonder. That's why the stories keep getting passed down.

That would've been a nice change, but it's not what Asaph says. He says the archers of Ephraim “…forgot what He had done, the wonders He had shown them.” Praise needs a memory to work with, and they let theirs go.
Taking notes sounds responsible, baker, but that's not what Asaph says. The archers of Ephraim “…forgot what He had done, the wonders He had shown them.” Forgot is the word he uses.

I see why you'd go there, but the sun never shows up in this verse. Asaph says, “He split the sea and brought them through; He set the waters upright like a wall.” The sea was split, and the waters stood upright. No sunshine plan, just God.

Right, no sun and no drying up in Asaph's telling. He says, “He split the sea and brought them through; He set the waters upright like a wall.” God split it, and the waters stood up. That's a different kind of wonder altogether.

explanations.answer: A cloud by day and fire by night
explanations.explanation: That's it: “He led them with a cloud by day and with a light of fire all night.” A cloud by day and a light of fire all night. Day and night, God covered the whole shift.

explanations.answer: An angel walking ahead of them
explanations.explanation: An angel would be a fine tour guide, friend, but Asaph doesn't mention one in this verse. He says, “He led them with a cloud by day and with a light of fire all night.” So the answer is a cloud for the day and a light of fire for the night.

explanations.answer: A star shining in the east
explanations.explanation: Stars are lovely, and I've got a whole sky full of them, friend. But Asaph doesn't mention one here. He says, “He led them with a cloud by day and with a light of fire all night.” A cloud for daytime and a fire light for night.

Asaph says God “…split the rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink as abundant as the seas.” Then he adds, “He brought streams from the stone and made water flow down like rivers.” A rock, in the middle of a wilderness, pouring out rivers. I'd have stared at it for a week.

Fancy, but no. Asaph says God split the rocks and “…gave them drink as abundant as the seas.” He also says He “…brought streams from the stone and made water flow down like rivers.” It was water, plenty of it.

That would be a breakfast surprise, but Asaph doesn't say it. He says God “…brought streams from the stone and made water flow down like rivers.” Out of those split rocks came water, as abundant as the seas.

Asaph says, “They willfully tested God by demanding the food they craved.” The word is demanding, and it's not the same as asking. They were putting God to the test on purpose. That's a different thing than a hungry heart saying, 'Lord, we need help.'
Sharing would've been lovely, baker, but that's not what Asaph says. He says they “…willfully tested God by demanding the food they craved.” Demanding is the word he picks.
Refusing isn't the word Asaph uses, friend. He says they “…willfully tested God by demanding the food they craved.” Craved food, demanded food, and that's how they tested Him.

Right. They say, “When He struck the rock, water gushed out and torrents raged. But can He also give bread or supply His people with meat?” They mention the water, then ask about bread and meat. I think that question is where the doubt shows.
The sea isn't what they're doubting here. They talk about the rock and the water, then ask, “But can He also give bread or supply His people with meat?” The doubt is about bread and meat.

Crops don't come up in their question. They say, “When He struck the rock, water gushed out and torrents raged. But can He also give bread or supply His people with meat?” Bread or meat is what they're doubting.

Asaph says, “Therefore the LORD heard and was filled with wrath; so a fire was kindled against Jacob, and His anger flared against Israel…” The LORD heard what they said. Asaph gives the reason: “…they did not believe God or rely on His salvation.”
Not this time, friend. Asaph says the LORD heard and “…was filled with wrath…” A fire was kindled against Jacob, and His anger flared against Israel.

Asaph picks a different word. He says, “…the LORD heard and was filled with wrath; so a fire was kindled against Jacob, and His anger flared against Israel…” Wrath is the word he uses for what God felt.
Yes, and Asaph says it plainly. God's anger flared “…because they did not believe God or rely on His salvation.” The problem was a heart that wouldn't trust Him. That's the reason the verse gives.
Asaph does say it. His anger flared against Israel “…because they did not believe God or rely on His salvation.” Verse 22 gives that reason right after the anger in verse 21. It's in the text.
Asaph says, “He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven.” The doors of the heavens open, and food comes down. Manna is the food he names.
Hail would've been a rough lunch, baker. But Asaph says, “He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven.” What fell was food.
A snow day, but not quite. Asaph says God opened the doors of the heavens and “…rained down manna for them to eat…” He also gave them “…grain from heaven.” It was food, not weather.

Asaph says, “He rained meat on them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea.” That's a lot of birds, friend. Right before it, he says God stirred the east wind and drove the south wind by His might.
Locusts are a different swarm, friend. Asaph says, “He rained meat on them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea.” He says winged birds, and locusts don't come up.

FROGS falling out of the sky? Baker, I'd hide under my chef's hat and never come out. But this verse has feathers, not frogs. Asaph says, “He rained meat on them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea.” Winged birds, friend, so the answer is birds.
Not far at all, friend. Asaph says, “He felled them in the midst of their camp, all around their dwellings.” That's right in the middle of the camp, around their own dwellings. No long walk required.
Right. The verse says, “He felled them in the midst of their camp, all around their dwellings.” So it happened in the middle of the camp, around where the people lived. Not out in the distance.
Asaph says, “When He slew them, they would seek Him; they repented and searched for God.” Hard times pointed them back toward God. Searching is what the verse says they did.

Mocking is what you'd expect after all this, baker, but that's not the word Asaph uses. He says, “When He slew them, they would seek Him; they repented and searched for God.” Seek and search are the words he picks. Mock isn't one of them.
That's not in the verse. Asaph says, “When He slew them, they would seek Him; they repented and searched for God.” Seeking and searching are the words he uses.
I wish that were the ending, friend. But Asaph says, “Their hearts were disloyal to Him, and they were unfaithful to His covenant.” Even with all that seeking, he says their hearts weren't loyal.

Right. Asaph says, “Their hearts were disloyal to Him, and they were unfaithful to His covenant.” Just before that, he says they deceived Him with their mouths and lied to Him with their tongues. The words sounded good, but the hearts weren't loyal.

Asaph says, “And yet He was compassionate; He forgave their iniquity and did not destroy them.” The hearts were disloyal, and still God was compassionate. I know what it is to be handed grace I didn't earn, friend.

explanations.answer: Waits for them to bring an offering
explanations.explanation: Asaph doesn't mention an offering. He says, “And yet He was compassionate; He forgave their iniquity and did not destroy them.” God is the one acting here. He forgave.

explanations.answer: Sends a prophet to warn them
explanations.explanation: No prophet shows up in these verses, baker. Asaph says, “And yet He was compassionate; He forgave their iniquity and did not destroy them.” Forgiving and sparing is what God does.
Yes, and it's a gentle line in a hard story. Asaph says, “He often restrained His anger and did not unleash His full wrath.” Often, he says, not once. That tells me something about the heart of God.
It's in the text, friend. Asaph says, “He often restrained His anger and did not unleash His full wrath.” That's right after he says God forgave their iniquity and did not destroy them.

Asaph says, “He remembered that they were but flesh, a passing breeze that does not return.” God knew exactly what they were made of. And no, that's not an excuse, it's what the verse says He remembered.
Not quite, baker. Asaph says they were unfaithful to His covenant (Psalm 78:37). What God remembered, he says, is “…that they were but flesh, a passing breeze that does not return.”

Battle strength isn't what Asaph says God remembered. He says, “He remembered that they were but flesh, a passing breeze that does not return.” That's the verse's answer, and it doesn't mention strength.
